zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Secondary lexical reference: *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ The BnF scan remains the primary evidence; review corrections and chosen readings are distinguished in the line notes.

lines.note: Rǒrô introduces an example of living banished or withdrawn. The scan restores the complete headword, the example Rǒrôiuru, and Eſtar deſterrado from the severely garbled OCR; the first and second vowel marks are respectively caron and circumflex.

runs.text: & recolhido ſem ſair a publico, nem ter de-

lines.note: Continues the withdrawn-life definition: remaining secluded, not appearing in public, and having no dealings with the world. The scan reads ſair, not the OCR ſamr; the printed de- leads into uer below.
Completes ter deuer com o mundo, having dealings with the world. The archaic wording and physical split are retained rather than rewritten as modern Portuguese.
Rôrôtoxite is an adverbial expression for being solitary. Both visible headword marks are circumflexes, unlike the first caron of the entry above; Adu. belongs to the italic grammatical explanation.

runs.text: & recolhido ſẽ tratar com a gente como ve-

lines.note: Expands the solitary manner as remaining secluded without dealing with people. The abbreviated ſẽ is preserved, and the comparison with old people continues after ve-.
Completes the comparison with old people and sufferers from melancholy. The Portuguese describes a manner of withdrawal, not a second Japanese lemma; the historical malenconia is retained.

runs.text: Hũa doença como etica, ou tiſica.

lines.note: Rǒſai names a wasting illness, compared in the source to hectic disease or phthisis. This is a historical gloss rather than a modern diagnosis; the abbreviation Hũa and both long ſ forms are preserved.

The verb Roſai means asking for alms, food, or sustenance. The scan restores initial R, the carons on its abbreviated forms, and the words comer and ſuſtẽtação; no modern expansion is substituted for the abbreviation.
The noun Roſai appears in the construction Roſaiuo itaſu, with the same alms-seeking meaning as the preceding verb. Vt and Idem are italic apparatus, while the full Japanese example is upright.

runs.text: Peßoa q̃ pede eſmola, ou ſuſtẽtação.

lines.note: Roſainin denotes someone who asks for alms or sustenance. The Portuguese retains both the q̃ abbreviation and the abbreviated syllable in ſuſtẽtação, rather than silently expanding either.
Rǒſo means an old rat, explicitly paraphrased by Voitaru nezumi. The final S. is the upright written-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese definition.
Roſǒ is a blue pigment, explained by Auoi yenogu. The scan restores initial R and muito; its final vowel has a caron, whereas the first o is unmarked.
Completes the blue-pigment gloss by specifying its use in painting. This continuation belongs to Roſǒ and introduces no new Japanese text.
Rǒſô is an aged religious person or Buddhist monk, paraphrased by Voita fijiri. The two vowel marks differ: caron first, circumflex second; the abbreviation in Bõzo is retained.

This separate Rôſô concerns a monk's clothing, as Sôno coromo explains. Both vowel marks are circumflexes. On the second pass the broken medial type is read as long ſ: its detached head lies to the right of the lower shaft, unlike an i dot. The supplied NINJAL entry 213a10 corroborates the lexical identification, not the typography.
Completes the definition as the dress or habit of a Buddhist monk. Bonzo is part of the Portuguese explanation, not a separate romanized Japanese citation.
Rǒſocu, explained by Voitaru axi, concerns the weakened legs of an old person. The Portuguese reads Velho, correcting the OCR Vello, and continues the person's limited walking ability below.
Completes the inability to walk far and begins an example using Rǒſocu. The paragraph mark and the printed hyphen after gozaruni are retained in their physical positions.
The example says that because of old age and weakness the speaker cannot come or go. Yotte continues the divided construction from the preceding line; Por quanto begins the Portuguese rendering.

runs.text: ſou ja velho, & fraco dos pees não poßo ir.

lines.note: Completes the speaker's explanation: already old and weak in the feet, unable to go. The scan has a word boundary between dos and pees; the historical pees and poßo are preserved.
Rǒſui means declining with age, paraphrased by Voi votorô. The Portuguese reads debilitando, not debititando, and includes a final ampersand linking the following continuation.
Completes the description as wearing away with old age. The scan prints gaſtandoſe continuously, so the provisional internal space is removed without modernizing its spelling.
Rotai is an ass's belly, explicitly paraphrased by Robano fara. Initial R replaces the OCR B, and the final upright S. marks written usage.

Rǒtai means an old person, equated with Toxi yori. The second pass resolves the faint mark as a caron: its surviving strokes descend to a low vertex, unlike the clear circumflex in the architectural Rôtai below. The supplied NINJAL entry 213a14 corroborates this scan-grounded reading.
Rôtai here denotes an elevated structure, paraphrased by Yagurano vtena. The Portuguese begins with tall houses; this is distinct from the preceding old-person entry despite the similar lettering.
Completes the architectural definition with towers inhabited by people. The historical singular mora with gente is retained as printed.
Rǒtaqe means beauty, followed by an example describing a beautiful woman. The scan reads Fermuſura, not Fermuſara; the nasalized võ- and its printed hyphen are preserved before the continuation.
Completes the divided Japanese word for woman and translates the example as a beautiful woman. The source's Molher and fermoſa spellings are retained.
Rotô is the edge of a road, directly explained by Michino fotori. The first o is unmarked and the final vowel bears a circumflex; the Japanese paraphrase is upright.
The example means standing beside the road. The Portuguese begins the equivalent standing or being on one's feet and continues on the following physical row.

runs.text: pee junto do caminho. ¶ Item, permet. An-

lines.note: Completes standing by the road, then introduces a figurative sense. Permet. is the source's metaphor label, and An- begins Andar on the next line.

runs.text: dar deſagaſalhado como pobre ſem caſa, &c.

lines.note: Completes the figurative explanation: wandering without shelter like a poor person without a house. The physical split An-/dar and the historical deſagaſalhado remain unchanged.
Rǒuô means an old man, paraphrased by Voitaru voqina. The scan restores initial R rather than B and preserves the distinct caron and circumflex on the two long vowels.
Rǒuoxǒ names a rank or dignity held by elderly Buddhist monks. The Portuguese description continues by identifying the tradition in the following row.

Completes the description as a dignity among the Ienxus, referring to the Zen tradition. Native enlargement confirms a capital I rather than OCR lowercase l. The surrounding Portuguese and the name remain in the supplied italic styling; Ienxus is flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Rôxa is glossed as imprisoned or incarcerated. The circumflex distinguishes this entry's written form from the old-person headword directly below.
Rǒxa denotes an old person, paraphrased by Voitaru mono. Its visible caron is retained rather than conflated with the preceding Rôxa.
Roxen denotes travel money, explained by Michino tçucai jeni. The Portuguese begins an alternative description using small coins on the next row; the Japanese paraphrase remains upright.
Completes the travel-money gloss with caxas for the journey. Caxas is the historical coin term in the Portuguese explanation, not modern boxes; the source spelling pera is retained.

runs.text: Embarcação que tẽ camara, ou varãda.

lines.note: Rôxẽ denotes a vessel with a cabin or raised covered space. The headword's final nasal abbreviation and the Portuguese tẽ and varãda are retained exactly rather than expanded.
Roxet concerns news heard along the road, paraphrased by Michino ſǒ. The small mark after i is read as a comma; the headword and Japanese explanatory words remain upright.

This Rôxet denotes winter-month snow, explained by Xiuaſuno yuqi. The Portuguese visibly starts vnde-cima, which is retained despite its discrepancy with the usual identification of Xiuaſu; the transcription does not silently correct the source's month number.
Completes the source's statement about the eleventh moon or month. The final S. is upright written-register apparatus, distinct from the italic Portuguese wording.
Roxi means a road or journey; the example describes talking along the way. The scan restores initial R and the paragraph mark, while the complete Japanese example remains on this physical row.
Translates the preceding example as conversing while coming along the road. Praticar has its historical conversational sense here, and pello is preserved.
Rǒxi and its abbreviated forms denote growing old. The long ſ in ſuru and the source spelling Enuelhecer are retained rather than modernized.
Rǒxin is an old retainer or servant, paraphrased by Voitaru xinca. The scan restores R and its caron from the OCR Boxin, and the written-register label S. is upright.
This Rǒxin means an aged or tired body, paraphrased by the continuously printed Voitarumi. It differs from the old-retainer entry at the foot of the preceding column; initial R replaces the OCR B.
Completes canſado, tired or worn out, in the preceding old-body definition. The long ſ and the physical word division are preserved.

Roxit and Rôxit are alternative forms for nocturnal emission during dreams. The linking l is the historical alternative-form marker, not a Japanese syllable; both full headwords are upright and the circumflex belongs only to the second form.
Rǒxô contrasts old and young people, as Voitari and vacaxi explain. The Portuguese mancebos is divided after man-, and the headword retains a first caron and final circumflex.
Completes mancebos, young men, in the old-and-young pair. This is a continuation of the preceding definition rather than a separate entry.
This separate Rǒxô is an old pine tree, directly paraphrased by Voimatçu. The scan reads Pinheiro, correcting the OCR Finheiro.
Rôxǒ means the top of a tower or raised defensive structure, paraphrased by Yagurano vye. Its first circumflex and final caron are the reverse of those in the preceding headwords.
Completes the architectural alternatives as a platform or tower. The historical term baileu is kept rather than replaced by a modern architectural label.

runs.text: Fraqueza, & canſaço por via do tra-

lines.note: Rǒxǒ denotes weakness and fatigue caused by work. Both vowel marks are carons; the Portuguese trabalho is divided after tra-.
Completes trabalho, establishing labor as the cause of the preceding exhaustion. The physical word division is retained.
Rǒyacu means good medicine, paraphrased by Yoqi cuſuri. Vt introduces the proverbial example on the following row; this is the dictionary's historical lexical explanation, not medical advice.
The proverb says that good medicine tastes bitter in the mouth. The Japanese sentence remains intact on this row, while the Portuguese mezinha is divided after me-.

runs.text: zinha he amargoſa na boca. Acomodaſe

lines.note: Completes the literal proverb and begins its figurative application. The scan prints Acomodaſe as one word, removing the OCR space after Ac; amargoſa retains the long ſ.

runs.text: aos bõs conſelhos que ſão mal ouuidos.

lines.note: Explains the proverb as applying to good advice that is unwelcome to its hearers. The nasal abbreviation bõs and historical ouuidos are preserved.

runs.text: Rǒyei. i, Vtauo yomi, guinzuru coto.

lines.note: Rǒyei concerns reciting or chanting verse. After the second pass, the extremely faint character after Vt is provisionally read as a in Vtauo: low traces remain but no clear i dot, and the resulting phrase explains reading poems. This choice is explicitly uncertain rather than an unmarked normalization. The Portuguese Fazer is divided here without a clearly printed hyphen.

Completes Fazer and describes singing or savoring verses. The source's separation cantando os and the explicit hyphen after ſaboreandoſe are retained, even though they do not match modern hyphenation conventions.

runs.text: nelles. ¶ Item, Hum certo liuro de poeſia.

lines.note: Finishes savoring the verses and adds a second Rǒyei sense, a particular book of poetry. The paragraph sign is restored and the source's capital Hum is kept.
Royen denotes the wooden surround of a hearth, paraphrased by Irorino camachi. The Portuguese begins describing pieces of wood laid in a frame; this is distinct from the signal-fire entry below.

runs.text: quadro nas bordas do fogão da caſa.

lines.note: Completes the hearth-surround definition: a square frame at the edges of the household hearth. The scan has f in fogão, not the OCR's long ſ.

Rǒyen denotes a signal fire or smoke, explicitly explained by Aizzuno qemuri. Enlarged second-pass comparison confirms the faint caron and the separate short hyphen after a, which begins aleuanta on the next row.

runs.text: leuanta pera dar ſinal, ou rebate.

lines.note: Completes the description of a fire raised to give a signal or alarm. The source spelling leuanta and the word rebate are preserved.
Rǒyeqi is illustrated by Rǒyeqiſuru, meaning to be weakened. The Japanese verbal construction is continuous in the scan, and the Portuguese debilitado is divided after debilita-.
Completes debilitado and adds weak as an equivalent description. This remains the continuation of the preceding Rǒyeqi example.
Rǒyǔ is an aged companion, paraphrased by Voitaru tomo. The first long vowel and final long u have carons, and the Portuguese velho is divided after ve-.

runs.text: lho: ou companhia de homem velho.

lines.note: Completes old companion and adds the companionship of an old man as another way of construing the expression. The colon separating these alternatives is retained.
Rǒzocu is an aged thief, directly paraphrased by Voitaru nuſubito. The Portuguese velho is divided after ve-.
Completes the literal old-thief gloss and adds a figurative sense, an experienced thief. The paragraph sign, Itẽ abbreviation, and metaphor label are preserved.

runs.text: O Soldar hum ferro, ou metal com

lines.note: Rǒzzuqe denotes soldering one piece of iron or metal to another. The doubled z of the headword and the source's capital Soldar are retained.
Completes the joining of one metal piece with another. This is the final body row of the R-before-O section; the heading below begins a new alphabetical section.

runs.text: Hum vaſo, ou panella de barro, em

lines.note: RV, with an enlarged initial R and capital V used for u, names an earthen vessel for melting metal. The OCR omitted the initial R; it is restored with two-line initial layout rather than treated as a separate row or headword V.

runs.text: que fundem prata, ou outro metal. ¶

lines.note: Completes the vessel's use for melting silver or other metal, then begins the related term Ru-ire. This physical row is indented beside the enlarged R; the paragraph mark and final hyphen are preserved.

runs.text: Liga que ſe deita neſta panella na

lines.note: Completes Ru-ire and begins its gloss as an alloying material added to silver in this vessel. The Japanese fragment remains on this row rather than being joined physically to Ru above.
Completes the Ru-ire definition by specifying that the added material goes into the silver. It belongs to the alloying entry rather than the following Ruberi.

runs.text: Quebras da prata q̃ ſe funde neſta pa

lines.note: Ruberi denotes losses in silver during melting in this vessel. The abbreviated q̃ is retained, and panella begins as pa at the line end without an invented hyphen.

runs.text: nella quando lhe botão a liga.

lines.note: Completes panella and specifies that the losses occur when alloying material is added. The historical botão is preserved rather than modernized to botam.

runs.text: Eſcorias que ficão de miſtura com a

lines.note: Rucaſu denotes slag or dross remaining mixed with ash after silver is melted. The scan restores initial R from OCR B, and the definition continues below.

runs.text: cinza de pois da prata fundida.

lines.note: Completes the slag definition with ash left after the melting of silver. Here the source visibly separates de pois, unlike the continuous depois on the preceding page; that difference is preserved.
Rucat denotes torn or patched clothing, with the Japanese explanatory words Tçuzzuri, ru. The Portuguese remendado is divided after remenda-, and the Japanese forms are not silently expanded.
Completes remendado, patched, in the ragged-clothing definition. The physical continuation and abbreviated etcetera are preserved.

Rufu means spreading or becoming widespread, equated with Firomaru. The final vowel of apparent couſo is retained as printed rather than normalized to couſa; the Portuguese continues with another equivalent below.
Completes the spreading sense and gives an example in which a teaching spreads through the world. The paragraph sign is restored, and the Japanese sentence stays in upright type on its original row.
Translates the example as the diffusion of a doctrine in the world. The abbreviation algũa and historical doctrina are retained, including the scan's connected ct type.
Rui means a kind or category, explained by Tagu-i. Two separate dots are visible after Rui and a hyphen within Tagu-i; both unusual printed details are retained rather than normalized.

Ruibiǒ denotes illness of the same kind. The worn initial of the explanatory phrase is read as T, with support from the visible Tagu-i immediately above. The second pass confirms the angular v in Tagvino, with no descending y tail; this printed spelling is retained rather than silently normalized to Taguino. The damaged initial remains a minor caveat.
Completes meſma laya, the same kind, in the preceding illness definition. The following signature and catchword are page furniture, not additional body rows.

zones.label: Printed signature
zones.note: Centered below column 2, on the same baseline as the catchword.

lines.note: The letter-spaced H h h is the printer's gathering signature. The original combined furniture ID is retained for this part of the baseline.

The far-right Ruichô. is a catchword, not part of the signature or the preceding illness definition. The weakly printed u is retained from the supplied reading; the final circumflex and full stop are visible.
